oppose_rescission_weaken_cra.label: Oppose rescinding or weakening CRA
oppose_rescission_weaken_cra.definition: General opposition to rescinding the 2023 rule and weakening CRA accountability, transparency and community obligations, including claims it benefits banks over communities.

support_proposal_burden_relief.label: Support proposal and burden reduction
support_proposal_burden_relief.definition: Support for rescission and for simplifying CRA, cutting compliance cost, recordkeeping and complexity, especially for community banks.

withdraw_or_delay_proposal.label: Withdraw, delay or reissue proposal
withdraw_or_delay_proposal.definition: Calls to withdraw, suspend, restart or delay the rulemaking, including pending impact analysis or recent housing legislation.

comment_period_process.label: Comment period and procedural concerns
comment_period_process.definition: Requests to extend the comment period and concerns about APA notice, insufficient information, proposal complexity and unexplained departure from the 2023 rule.

lack_of_impact_analysis.label: Lack of impact and cost-benefit analysis
lack_of_impact_analysis.definition: Criticism that agencies did not analyze effects on LMI, rural, minority and redlined communities, housing and lending, or that cost and paperwork estimates were flawed.

interagency_inconsistency_fed.label: Interagency inconsistency and Fed absence
interagency_inconsistency_fed.definition: Concerns about divergent rules across OCC, FDIC and Federal Reserve, repeated rule changes, instability, and calls for a uniform, durable interagency rule.

asset_size_thresholds.label: Asset size thresholds for bank categories
asset_size_thresholds.definition: Positions on raising, keeping or indexing thresholds for small, intermediate and large banks, including $1B, $3.252B, $10B and $30B options.

bank_reclassification_loss_of_coverage.label: Banks reclassified and losing CRA obligations
bank_reclassification_loss_of_coverage.definition: Concerns that raised thresholds move banks into lighter categories, removing tests, data reporting and local obligations, including branchless or digital banks.

investment_test_cd_tests.label: Investment test and CD evaluation for banks
investment_test_cd_tests.definition: Concerns about eliminating the standalone investment test and weakening community development tests for large and intermediate banks.

cd_benchmarks_strategic_plans.label: CD benchmarks and strategic plan option
cd_benchmarks_strategic_plans.definition: Views on the 0.625% Tier 1 capital benchmark, other quantitative benchmarks becoming ceilings, and strategic plan guardrails, process and public participation.

economic_dev_infrastructure_eligibility.label: Broadened economic development and infrastructure credit
economic_dev_infrastructure_eligibility.definition: Concerns about removing the economic development purpose test and crediting infrastructure or other activities with little LMI benefit.

cd_definitions_eligible_activities.label: CD definitions, NOAH and qualifying activities
cd_definitions_eligible_activities.definition: Comments on defining and adding qualifying activities such as NOAH, SBA 504, CDFIs, disaster resilience, special purpose credit programs, financial education and illustrative lists.

confirmation_transition_implementation.label: Confirmation process and implementation timing
confirmation_transition_implementation.definition: Comments on advance confirmation of activities, examiner guidance, effective dates, transition periods and treatment of prior-period or pending commitments.

grant_indirect_cost_cap.label: 15% indirect cost cap on grants
grant_indirect_cost_cap.definition: Objections to or comments on the 15 percent cap on indirect or overhead costs for grants receiving CRA credit, including definitions and calculation base.

grant_eligibility_documentation.label: Grant eligibility and documentation burden
grant_eligibility_documentation.definition: Concerns about limits on credit for general operating, capacity-building and other grants, and documentation burdens that lead banks to cut or redirect grants away from small nonprofits.

nonprofit_cdfi_partnerships.label: Impacts on CDFIs, nonprofits and partnerships
nonprofit_cdfi_partnerships.definition: Importance of CRA incentives for bank capital, grants and partnerships with CDFIs, nonprofits, intermediaries and mission-driven lenders, and effects of losing them.

affordable_housing_lihtc_effects.label: Affordable housing and LIHTC/NMTC investment effects
affordable_housing_lihtc_effects.definition: Concerns that weakened CRA reduces bank demand and pricing for LIHTC, Housing Credit and NMTC equity and reduces affordable housing production and funding.

reduced_cd_activity_overall.label: Reduced community development activity overall
reduced_cd_activity_overall.definition: Projected declines in bank community development lending, investment and services and weaker incentives for private capital flow.

service_test_deposit_branches.label: Service test, deposit products and branches
service_test_deposit_branches.definition: Concerns about dropping deposit products and narrowing retail services review, branch closures and deserts, and access for unbanked and underbanked households.

assessment_areas_outside_aa.label: Assessment areas and credit outside them
assessment_areas_outside_aa.definition: Comments on assessment area definitions, geographic flexibility, credit for community development outside assessment areas, digital banking and CRA deserts.

retail_lending_major_product_lines.label: Retail lending test and major product lines
retail_lending_major_product_lines.definition: Comments on limiting review to top product lines, consumer lending evaluation, complexity definitions, purpose test for small business loans, and risk of hiding lending gaps.

data_reporting_transparency.label: CRA data collection, reporting and transparency
data_reporting_transparency.definition: Concerns about losing small business, small farm, community development and other CRA data, Section 1071 overlap, and public visibility into lending gaps.

fair_lending_redlining_enforcement.label: Fair lending, redlining and discrimination evidence
fair_lending_redlining_enforcement.definition: Concerns about narrowing discrimination evidence for rating downgrades, redlining accountability, consumer protection enforcement and merger or consolidation review.

harm_lmi_minority_communities.label: Harm to LMI, minority and underserved communities
harm_lmi_minority_communities.definition: General concerns and CRA's anti-redlining purpose, with impacts on LMI, minority, disabled and limited-English people, small businesses and local communities.

rural_tribal_disaster_impacts.label: Rural, Tribal and disaster-area impacts
rural_tribal_disaster_impacts.definition: Effects on rural and small communities and requests to recognize Indian Country, Indian Housing Plans, Tribal engagement and disaster areas.

small_business_lending.label: Small business lending and SBA programs
small_business_lending.definition: Comments on small business credit gaps, SBA 504 and SBA-aligned thresholds, revenue thresholds and technical assistance.

extend_cra_nonbanks.label: Extending CRA to nonbanks and credit unions
extend_cra_nonbanks.definition: Calls to cover credit unions, fintechs and other nonbanks under CRA.

off_topic.label: Off-topic or irrelevant comments
off_topic.definition: Comments unrelated to the CRA rule, such as fraud claims, remittance taxes, digital currency or personal disputes.

other.label: Other issues
other.definition: Issues that fit none of the canonical issues.

comments.name: Kenneth Thomas
comments.type_basis: Submitted under his own name with no organization listed, writing from personal experience and describing himself as an individual submitter.
comments.overall_quote: The July 31, 2026 OCC/FDIC CRA proposal, OCC-2026-0694, is very disappointing because it fails to address the central reason CRA modernization became necessary in the first place
comments.summary: The commenter objects that the proposal keeps CRA assessment areas tied to physical branches. He says this leaves communities that supply deposits to branchless and digital banks without a reinvestment obligation, a problem he calls "weblining." He urges the agencies to adopt a deposit-based assessment area rule with a 5 percent threshold, modeled on the OCC's 2020 rule. He also suggests a simple approach: keep the 1995 regulations and add that rule plus useful elements of the 2023 rule.
key_asks: Request comment on a targeted deposit-based assessment-area framework, including a modern 5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule like the OCC's 2020 rule.
Keep the 1995 regulations and update them with the 5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule.
Add the best ideas from the rescinded 2023 rule, such as the list of qualified CD activities.

provisions.quote: By retaining a framework centered on physical facilities, the proposal misses an important opportunity to modernize CRA for the realities of digital banking.
maintain the current 1995 regs and update them with the 5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule and the best ideas from the rescinded 2023 CRA Final Rule

comments.commenter_subtype: private individual (former Senate staff/economist, Ph.D.)

sources.quote: like my home community of South Florida

issues.raw_label: Failure to address digital banking
issues.quote: it fails to address the central reason CRA modernization became necessary in the first place: the growth of digital and branchless banking since CRA’s last major reform in 1995.

issues.raw_label: Deposit-based assessment areas needed
issues.quote: the OCC and FDIC should reconsider this serious omission and specifically request comment on a targeted deposit-based assessment-area framework

issues.raw_label: 5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule
issues.quote: a bank has a CRA reinvestment requirement in any area sourcing 5% or more of its deposits.

issues.raw_label: Branchless banks escaping CRA obligations
issues.quote: leaves those communities without a corresponding CRA reinvestment obligation.

issues.raw_label: Weblining of deposits from communities
issues.quote: the comparable danger is what I have labeled "weblining," namely the ability of branchless banks to gather substantial deposits electronically from communities

issues.raw_label: South Florida deposits without reinvestment
issues.quote: There is no commensurate reinvestment requirement for the more than $100 billion of estimated deposits these branchless banks harvest from South Florida.

issues.raw_label: Retain 2020 OCC deposit-based approach
issues.quote: Comptroller Otting’s 2020 OCC rule demonstrated that this problem can be addressed in a targeted manner with deposit-based assessment area

issues.raw_label: Maintain 1995 regs with updates
issues.quote: maintain the current 1995 regs and update them with the 5% Deposit Reinvestment Rule and the best ideas from the rescinded 2023 CRA Final Rule

comments.name: San Joaquin Valley Housing Collaborative
comments.type_basis: Self-described regional nonprofit whose members include affordable housing developers, local governments, lenders, and community organizations in California's San Joaquin Valley.
comments.overall_quote: We recognize and support the agencies' goals of clarity, continuity, and reduced burden for community banks. But these two provisions would not reduce burden on communities.
comments.summary: The Collaborative, a San Joaquin Valley housing nonprofit, objects to two provisions: reclassifying banks between $1.65B and $10B as intermediate banks outside the investment test, and the limits on CD grants including the 15 percent overhead documentation. It argues these would reduce LIHTC investment and grant support in a capital-scarce region, while voicing general support for clarity, continuity, and reduced burden for community banks.
key_asks: Retain a community development investment component for banks above the current large bank threshold, or at minimum give LIHTC and other CD investments distinct, meaningful recognition in the intermediate bank evaluation.
Withdraw the 15 percent overhead documentation requirement for CD grants.
Preserve CRA consideration for grants, including general operating support, to organizations with a community development purpose.

provisions.quote: If these banks can receive the same CRA consideration for ordinary market-rate lending, many will have little reason to continue purchasing housing credits.
The 15 percent overhead figure has no basis in how effective nonprofits actually operate, and it penalizes small rural organizations that run lean

comments.name: For Small Business Only LLC
comments.type_basis: The commenter describes itself as a Virginia LLC acting as a technical-assistance and capital-readiness intermediary for small businesses, working with nonprofits and banks.
comments.overall_quote: For Small Business Only LLC strongly supports the agencies' proposed amendments to the Community Reinvestment Act regulations.
comments.summary: The commenter, a small-business technical-assistance and capital-readiness intermediary, strongly supports the proposal. It focuses on the recognition of technical assistance, financial literacy, direct nonprofit grants with assessment-area nexus, and the 15% indirect-cost cap. It asks for implementation clarifications on grant documentation, including for new nonprofits, curriculum licensing fees, reporting costs and related-party safeguards.
key_asks: Retain the economic development category covering technical assistance for small businesses and farms, and preserve the 15% indirect-cost guardrail in the final rule.

Clarify the 15% grant rules: allow newly formed nonprofits without a Form 990 to document compliance through budgets, policies and attestation. Treat arm's-length curriculum license fees and outcome-reporting costs as direct costs. Allow related-party costs with safeguards. Confirm that 2 CFR part 200-comparable cost allocation methods are acceptable.
Encourage a standardized but scalable evidence package for grant recipients, and keep making clear that technical assistance does not require or guarantee a subsequent loan.

provisions.quote: FSBO supports the proposed 15% indirect-cost limit for community-development grants made by large banks.
FSBO particularly supports the proposed economic-development category covering technical assistance and support services for qualifying small businesses and farms.

comments.name: Project Read (joint letter with Elevate Utah and Wasatch Homeless Health Care dba Fourth Street Clinic)
comments.type_basis: The letter is signed by leaders of Utah nonprofits (Project Read, Elevate Utah, Fourth Street Clinic) that describe themselves as nonprofits serving low- and moderate-income Utahns and receiving CRA grants.
comments.overall_quote: We respectfully urge the OCC and FDIC to remove the proposed 15% indirect-cost cap or substantially revise it to recognize legitimate, reasonable, and federally accepted nonprofit cost structures.
comments.summary: Three Utah nonprofits argue that the proposed 15% indirect-cost ceiling on community-development grant recipients misuses the federal de minimis rate. They say it would push banks to favor larger organizations over small local nonprofits, create undefined measurement and compliance burdens, and conflict with the Federal Reserve's standards. They ask the agencies to remove the cap or substantially revise it, and they use Project Read as an example.
key_asks: Remove the fixed 15% indirect-cost ceiling on community-development grant recipients, or if one is kept, define indirect costs and the measurement base clearly.

If a standard is retained, add a safe harbor for smaller nonprofits, keep CRA consideration for general operating and capacity-building grants, reduce documentation burdens, and provide a transition period for multi-year grants.
Coordinate with the Federal Reserve Board to keep a consistent interagency standard for community-development grants, or explain how the agencies will handle the divergence.

provisions.quote: We respectfully ask the OCC and FDIC to remove the proposed fixed 15% indirect-cost ceiling.

comments.overall_quote: We support the OCC and FDIC's efforts to clarify CRA implementation and reduce regulatory burden and support several components of the proposed rule. However, we are concerned that some proposed changes, taken together, may not have the intended effect
comments.summary: NAAHL, an affordable housing lenders' alliance, supports several parts of the proposal. These include prior-period CD loan credit, an illustrative activity list, a prior-determination process, and Tribal land eligibility. It opposes higher asset thresholds, the grant restrictions, removing the economic development purpose test, and narrowing data reporting, and it asks for changes to the outside-assessment-area framework.
key_asks: Do not raise asset thresholds; keep CD responsibilities for banks of all sizes and maintain CRA-specific thresholds.
Drop the 15 percent grant cap and documentation requirements, and keep grants eligible based on community development purpose.

Replace the numeric outside-AA test with a standard based on prior satisfactory exam performance, keep the economic development purpose test, and maintain the 2016 Interagency Q&A with a 24-month transition.

provisions.quote: NAAHL does not endorse the proposed changes to bank asset thresholds.
We strongly oppose the proposed changes to grant making as unnecessarily burdensome and harmful to the community-based organizations that provide essential services and rely on operating grants.

Banks' record of providing a wide range of products and services, including deposit services, to LMI customers should remain part of a bank's record of helping to meet community credit needs through services.
The agencies should not adopt a radius-based standard to determine assessment areas.
While we support the agencies' efforts to add clarity, we are concerned that the framework under Option 1, as proposed, may not have the intended effect.
Economic development activities should continue to meet a "purpose test" demonstrating a benefit to LMI individuals or geographies.
We support allowing banks to utilize technology to share information and their public file at the bank's option.
We support the agencies' efforts to provide additional clarity on elements of an impactful strategic plan.
we urge you to decouple data reporting from the large bank designation so that communities, lenders, and researchers do not lose vital insights into community development activity and needs.
Provide favorable consideration for financing in partnership with community development financial institutions (CDFIs) nationwide;

comments.commenter_subtype: National affordable housing lenders alliance (banks, CDFIs, and other lenders and investors)

comments.name: National Sign-on Letter (coalition of community development, affordable housing, and nonprofit organizations)
comments.type_basis: The letter is signed by hundreds of affordable housing developers, CDFIs, nonprofits and housing authorities who describe building affordable housing and financing small businesses and community facilities.
comments.overall_quote: proposed changes to CRA, taken together, could significantly reduce community development activity and the lending, investment, grants, and other critical resources available for low- and moderate-income communities.
comments.summary: A national sign-on letter from hundreds of housing, CDFI and nonprofit organizations warns that the proposed changes together would reduce community development lending, investment and grants for low- and moderate-income communities. It urges the agencies to keep community development duties for banks of all sizes, preserve both loans and investments, protect grant support for nonprofits, and keep LMI focus, while saying it supports making CRA clearer and workable.
key_asks: Maintain community development responsibilities for banks of all sizes, rather than raising asset thresholds so that more banks are exempt
Preserve a strong, balanced role for both community development lending and investment in the evaluation framework
Protect grants to nonprofits without new burdensome restrictions or documentation, and keep a clear focus on low- and moderate-income people and communities

provisions.quote: Raising the asset thresholds that determine how banks are evaluated under CRA would significantly reduce the number of institutions subject to community development expectations.

comments.name: American Fintech Council
comments.type_basis: The letter is signed by AFC's Chief Policy Officer and describes AFC as a trade association of more than 150 fintech companies and innovative banks.
comments.overall_quote: The Proposed Rule advances several of those objectives. However, AFC recognizes that several of the changes under consideration by the Proposed Rule could adversely affect the CRA efforts of innovative banks
comments.summary: AFC, a fintech and innovative bank trade group, welcomes the proposal's aims of flexibility and reduced burden but asks for changes so that it does not harm innovative banks. It urges keeping the limited purpose bank designation and flexible strategic plans, a materiality-based major product line test, a safe harbor for the 15 percent grant cap, flexible outside-assessment-area community development credit, and streamlined data reporting.
key_asks: Preserve the limited purpose bank designation, treat the 5 percent incidental lending threshold as a rebuttable presumption, and keep strategic plans flexible with transition and grandfathering treatment.

Adopt a materiality-based major product line framework, restore the loan-to-deposit ratio language on other lending-related activities, and avoid adverse conclusions for nationwide or digital models with few in-area loans.

Treat the 15 percent indirect cost limit as a safe harbor, keep a flexible and attainable outside-assessment-area community development pathway, and align data reporting with Section 1071 and with sufficient implementation time.

provisions.quote: AFC strongly recommends that the agencies preserve the limited purpose (LP) bank designation.

AFC recognizes that the Proposed Rule would not provide for the assessment of deposit products, consistent with the agencies' position in pending litigation, and does not ask the agencies to revisit that position.
AFC recognizes the agencies' position that the CRA does not permit assessment of retail lending outside those areas and does not ask the agencies to extend CRA consideration to such lending.
The final rule should preserve a practical pathway for banks to receive CRA consideration for qualifying community development activities outside their facility-based assessment areas
AFC recommends that the agencies treat the proposed 15 percent indirect cost threshold as a safe harbor rather than an absolute limitation
an institution should not be required to collect and report information unless that information materially contributes to its CRA evaluation or serves a distinct and identifiable supervisory purpose.

comments.name: Developers Collaborative
comments.type_basis: The commenter describes itself as a Portland-based real estate developer and Maine's leading producer of affordable housing using Housing Credits. It is a developer rather than a nonprofit or CDFI, but it is the closest fit among the available types.
comments.overall_quote: We strongly encourage the OCC and FDIC to leave the thresholds as they currently stand under the 1995 CRA rule
comments.summary: The commenter is an affordable housing developer in Maine. It opposes raising the large bank threshold because reclassifying banks as intermediate would remove the investment test, which it says would lower Housing Credit equity pricing and cut affordable housing production, especially in rural areas. It prefers the existing thresholds, then the $3.252 billion alternative, and it calls the $30 billion alternative the worst option.

comments.overall_quote: I urge the agencies to revise the proposal to preserve comparable public lending information, consequential community-development examinations, and a documented connection between CRA consideration and community benefit.
comments.summary: An individual Texas commenter urges the agencies to revise the proposal to keep comparable annual small-business lending disclosure, consequential community-development exams, and documented LMI benefit. He asks for reasonable-cost documentation instead of the 15% grant overhead cap, a retained economic-development purpose test, and accountable infrastructure records, while supporting burden relief such as eliminating duplicative reporting.
key_asks: Retain annual small-business reporting for currently covered banks until a comparable public replacement (e.g., section 1071 data) is shown adequate, and publish a crosswalk.

Preserve distinct community-development review and require Satisfactory CD performance for a Satisfactory intermediate overall rating; replace the 15% indirect-cost ceiling with reasonable-cost documentation.

Retain the economic-development purpose test or an equivalent documented benefit standard, and require documented benefit records for infrastructure; publish institution- and geography-specific impact evidence.

provisions.quote: I ask the agencies to preserve distinct community-development review for banks currently subject to it or demonstrate equivalent scrutiny before changing their treatment.
I ask the agencies to retain annual reporting for currently covered banks until they demonstrate an adequate and timely public replacement.
replace the rigid ceiling with documented reasonable costs and demonstrable community-development benefits.
retain the purpose test or require an equivalent, proportionately documented benefit pathway
Retain the requirement of Satisfactory community-development performance for a Satisfactory intermediate overall rating

comments.commenter_subtype: individual commenter; university student and NCRC fellow, Grand Prairie, Texas

Nicholas D. Hawkins

issues.quote: Maintain consequential community-development examinations, including identifiable findings on loans, investments, grants, and services and a meaningful relationship to overall CRA ratings.

issues.quote: My concern is that an overall Satisfactory rating could communicate adequate responsiveness while the bank's community-development performance remains weaker.

issues.quote: The proposed thresholds and §§ 25.26 and 345.26 would move some banks into small-bank treatment without mandatory distinct community-development testing.

issues.quote: Replace the rigid 15% indirect-cost condition for qualifying large-bank grants with reasonable-cost documentation, proportionate accountability, and demonstrable community benefit.

issues.quote: illustrates the activity made visible by separate tests.

comments.name: Harborlight Homes
comments.type_basis: The letter says Harborlight Homes is a non-profit, Massachusetts-certified Community Development Corporation that develops affordable housing.
comments.overall_quote: We are concerned that several provisions of the proposed rule, particularly when considered together, could significantly weaken the regulatory framework supporting banks' engagement in these activities.
comments.summary: Harborlight Homes, a Massachusetts CDC, worries the proposal's higher asset thresholds and tighter treatment of grants would reduce bank lending, investment, and grants for affordable housing. It asks the agencies to keep the current thresholds or else preserve separate CD lending and investment tests, and to extend the comment period.
key_asks: Keep the current asset thresholds: Large over $1.649B, Intermediate $412M to $1.649B, Small under $412M.
If thresholds are raised, keep CD Investment and Lending assessed as separate, meaningful criteria for formerly Large Banks.
Extend the comment period by 60 to 90 days.

provisions.quote: we respectfully request that the OCC and FDIC preserve the dollar limits of banks in their current categories and testing requirements

We are very concerned about proposals that could make it more difficult for banks to receive CRA consideration for grants that support the operating capacity necessary to deliver community development outcomes.

comments.name: Independent Community Bankers of America
comments.type_basis: ICBA is a trade association representing community banks, and the letter is signed by its regulatory counsel and policy director.
comments.overall_quote: ICBA supports the Proposal and offers the following principal recommendations:
comments.summary: ICBA supports the proposal as a step toward a lending-focused, proportionate CRA framework for community banks. It backs higher asset thresholds, major product lines, facility-based assessment areas, optional outside-area credit and a website public file. It asks for higher thresholds, relief from the 15% grant cap, a single joint illustrative list, broader MDI/CDFI/mutual bank recognition, and harmonization with the Federal Reserve.
key_asks: Set the small bank threshold at $10 billion (or at least $5 billion) and the intermediate bank threshold at $30 billion.
Add a de minimis exception, small nonprofit exemption, and attestation safe harbor for the 15% indirect cost cap on grants, and a de minimis exception to the geographic flexibility standard.

Require a single, jointly maintained illustrative list of CD activities, and expand recognition of MDIs, CDFIs and mutual banks (presumption of CD purpose, complexity, geographic treatment equal to MDIs).
Finalize the rule jointly with the Federal Reserve, or allow a longer effective date.

provisions.quote: ICBA strongly supports modernizing the asset thresholds, which would increase the proportionality of the rule.
The proposed 15 percent cap on recipients' indirect costs would burden the small, local nonprofits that serve communities most directly.
ICBA supports this refocusing, which ties CRA examinations more closely to the lending that most directly meets community credit needs.
ICBA supports retaining an assessment area framework grounded in a bank's physical presence
ICBA supports this optional framework, which would allow banks to comply with the CRA more efficiently
Of the alternatives presented, Option 2 appears more comprehensive because it considers examination findings in addition to judicial orders and enforcement actions.
ICBA supports this approach. Most banks already maintain websites where customers can find information about their products, staff, operations, and regulatory status
ICBA supports discontinuing duplicative CRA small business data collection in favor of Section 1071 data to the fullest extent possible.
The agencies should therefore explicitly recognize support for all CDFIs as a qualifying community development activity
ICBA strongly supports codifying the illustrative list, which would promote transparency and give banks the confidence to plan and invest in their CRA programs.

Excluding deposit services from the evaluation of retail banking services could create a significant gap in the assessment of a bank's overall responsiveness to community needs.

comments.overall_quote: HPN is concerned that the changes to the asset thresholds proposed in Section IV.A of the NPR will significantly decrease investment in affordable housing at a time when housing affordability is a national issue.
comments.summary: HPN, a network of affordable housing developers and CDFIs, opposes the higher asset thresholds, the removal of the intermediate bank CD test minimum, and the 15 percent cap on CD grants. It supports including naturally occurring affordable housing (NOAH) in the definition. It worries that crediting middle-income housing in high-cost areas could dilute the focus on LMI communities.
key_asks: Retain the current intermediate bank rating structure requiring Satisfactory on both the lending and CD tests.
Retain the 1995 rule framework for general operating and capacity-building grants; if a 15 percent cap is kept, clearly define administrative costs.
Keep the focus on LMI communities and households, and add explicit examples of nonprofit-partnership affordable housing activities to the final rule.

provisions.quote: Under the proposed thresholds, 79.8 percent2 of banks would have no community development obligation while 416 banks would no longer be subject to the investment test
HPN opposes these limiting changes because grants can serve a wide array of important purposes for nonprofits and CDFIs in delivering investment and services into communities.
HPN recommends retaining the current rating structure, which requires intermediate banks to receive a Satisfactory rating on both the lending and CD tests to receive an overall Satisfactory rating.
HPN supports the NPR's inclusion of NOAH with rents affordable to LMI individuals being set at 30 percent of 80 percent AMI.

comments.commenter_subtype: affordable housing developer and CDFI network

comments.name: Bridgeway Capital
comments.type_basis: The letter describes Bridgeway as a US Treasury-certified CDFI in Pittsburgh that lends to small businesses and nonprofits in LMI communities.
comments.overall_quote: We are therefore concerned that several provisions in the proposal could weaken these incentives, reducing bank engagement with CDFIs and ultimately the flow of capital to the communities we serve.
comments.summary: Bridgeway, a CDFI, opposes the higher asset thresholds. It says they would shrink the pool of CRA-motivated bank capital and reduce CRA data available to CDFIs. It supports several provisions that could strengthen CD finance: flexible allocation of CD activities across assessment areas, credit for prior-period CD loans, and an illustrative list with advance confirmation of eligibility.
key_asks: Retain the current asset thresholds and reject all proposed alternatives.
Give CRA consideration to prior-period CD loans, using evaluation-period average balances and treating repeated renewals as a single exposure.
Establish an interagency illustrative list of CD activities and an advance-confirmation process with written rationales, reconsideration, public determinations, and stakeholder input.

provisions.quote: we ask that the agencies retain the current thresholds and reject all proposed alternatives.
Should more institutions be exempted from CRA reporting requirements, it will leave CDFIs like Bridgeway with less visibility into the capital needs in our communities.
We support greater flexibility in allocating CD activities that benefit or serve multiple assessment areas.
We strongly support providing CRA consideration for qualifying CD loans that remain outstanding from prior evaluation periods, similar to the existing treatment of prior-period investments.
We strongly support establishing a publicly available, non-exhaustive illustrative list of eligible CD activities and a formal process for advance confirmation of eligibility.

comments.type_basis: The comment asks for CDFI presumptions and grant treatment, and the signer is the president of PEOPLE TRUST in Little Rock. The comment never states what kind of organization PEOPLE TRUST is, so this type is a judgment call.
comments.overall_quote: We are concerned, however, that several changes would weaken the law's core obligation: the much higher asset thresholds, the optional community development test for intermediate banks, the removal of deposit services, the grant restrictions
comments.summary: The commenter supports some of the proposal's clarifications, including the illustrative list, the confirmation process, and the new Indian country and disaster categories. It opposes the higher asset thresholds, the grant limits, the removal of deposit services, and the dropped LMI job test, and it answers all 63 questions in detail. Its main request is a presumption of community development purpose for CDFI activity across all categories.

Reject the $1B/$10B thresholds, keep deposit services in the service test, and keep the LMI job requirement for economic development.
Replace the 15% grant cap with a negotiated rate or 25%, whichever is higher. Adopt Option B on discriminatory credit practices.

comments.name: Indiana Affordable Housing Council
comments.type_basis: Statewide membership organization of affordable housing developers, lenders, investors, and nonprofits dedicated to preserving and expanding affordable housing in Indiana.
comments.overall_quote: We strongly oppose the proposal to increase the large bank asset threshold from approximately $1.65 billion to $10 billion, which would eliminate the separate investment test for banks with assets between those levels.
comments.summary: The Indiana Affordable Housing Council strongly opposes raising the large bank threshold to $10 billion. It argues this would remove the investment test for many banks, weaken LIHTC investor demand and pricing, and reduce affordable housing equity, especially in rural Indiana.
key_asks: Retain the existing large bank asset threshold (about $1.65 billion) rather than raising it to $10 billion
Retain the separate investment test for banks between the current and proposed thresholds
Pursue regulatory burden reduction while preserving strong incentives for affordable housing investment

provisions.quote: We respectfully ask the agencies to retain the existing asset threshold and the separate investment test.
